steps.en: What you see: Tamponade is pressure, not size. The right atrium collapses in late diastole and the right ventricle collapses in early diastole because these low pressure chambers give way first. The inferior vena cava is dilated above 21 mm with below 50 percent collapse on sniffing. Mitral inflow falls sharply on inspiration while tricuspid inflow rises, an exaggerated see saw across the two sides.

Normal values with units: Inferior vena cava in tamponade. Dilated above 21 mm with collapse below 50 percent on a sniff suggests raised right atrial pressure around 15 mmHg.. Source: ASE 2019 transthoracic examination guideline, section on the inferior vena cava

Respiratory inflow variation. Mitral inflow fall above 25 percent on inspiration with a reciprocal tricuspid rise above 40 percent supports tamponade physiology.. Source: ASE 2019 transthoracic examination guideline, section on Doppler and haemodynamics

Pulsus paradoxus at the bedside. A systolic pressure fall above 10 mmHg on quiet inspiration supports tamponade and is checked with a manual cuff.. Source: ACEP emergency ultrasound guidance and international POCUS consensus, section on focused cardiac views

ECG and heart sound correlation ecg: Sinus tachycardia is almost always present. Low voltage with electrical alternans appears when a large effusion lets the heart swing. Atrial arrhythmia can follow compression of the chambers.
ECG and heart sound correlation sounds: Heart sounds are muffled with tachycardia. The jugular venous pressure is raised. Pulsus paradoxus above 10 mmHg on the bedside pulse is the clinical hallmark.

What to report: Which chambers collapse and in which phase of the cycle
Inferior vena cava size and collapse with the estimated right atrial pressure
Inflow variation across respiration with the numbers
Effusion size, position and any clot or fibrin that would hinder needle drainage
Red flags needing urgent referral: Hypotension with chamber collapse, needs immediate pericardial drainage by the senior team
Pulseless electrical activity with an effusion on the pulse check view, needs immediate drainage during resuscitation
Effusion with tuberculosis clues in an Indian patient such as lymph nodes or a chronic febrile illness, needs urgent workup alongside drainage
Pitfalls: After cardiac surgery blood clots hide behind one wall, so absence of a circumferential effusion never rules out tamponade.
Pulmonary hypertension stiffens the right side and can mask collapse, so integrate the vena cava and clinical signs.
Positive pressure ventilation reverses the respiratory pattern, so read inflow variation with the ventilator in mind.

todo.en: How to get it on the probe, step by step: Start subcostal in the supine patient and find the effusion with the right atrium and right ventricle.
Watch the right atrium through late diastole for inward collapse lasting more than one third of the cycle.
Watch the right ventricular free wall in early diastole for inward motion.
Record mitral and tricuspid inflow with pulsed wave Doppler across one full breath.
Measure the inferior vena cava 1 to 2 cm from the right atrium at rest and on a sniff.

Common mistakes and how to correct them: Calling systolic indenting of the atrium a tamponade sign. Fix: Check the ECG timing on the trace. True tamponade collapse is diastolic, systolic indenting has other causes.
Overreading inflow variation in a patient with laboured breathing. Fix: Ask about chronic lung disease and record across a calm breath. Forced breathing exaggerates normal variation.
Diagnosing tamponade from collapse alone in severe dehydration. Fix: Rescan after fluids and oxygen. A dehydrated patient can show collapse without tamponade.

remember.en: Act on tamponade as an emergency that needs urgent drainage.

q.en: When does the right ventricle collapse in tamponade?

why.en: The low pressure right ventricle gives way in early diastole when sac pressure exceeds chamber pressure.

q.en: Which vena cava finding supports tamponade?

o.en: Above 21 mm with below 50 percent collapse
Any size if the patient coughs

why.en: A dilated cava above 21 mm with below 50 percent collapse suggests raised right atrial pressure.

q.en: A hypotensive breathless patient shows right sided collapse with a large effusion. What next?

o.en: Start a beta blocker and observe

why.en: Hypotension with collapse is tamponade until proven otherwise and needs immediate drainage by the senior team.
